headline: Strait of Hormuz Crisis Drives WTI Above $100 as Canada Posts 0.1% GDP Growth and 84,000 Job Losses
executive_summary:
Commodities & Energy

The Strait of Hormuz has been effectively closed since approximately March 2, disrupting an estimated 20 million barrels per day of seaborne oil flows.104 WTI crude settled at US$102.88/bbl on March 30 — the first close above $100 since July 2022.104 Brent crude surged approximately 55% in March to US$112.78/bbl, a record monthly gain since the contract's 1988 inception.104 The Dallas Federal Reserve estimated a one-quarter closure could raise WTI to $98/bbl and reduce global GDP growth by 2.9 percentage points in Q2 2026.108 The project database tracks 63 oil and gas projects and 785 power and energy projects across Canada. Alberta accounts for 727 of these tracked projects.

Labour Market

Employment declined by 84,000 (-0.4%) in February, reversing Q4 2025 gains.144 Full-time positions fell 108,000 and private-sector employment dropped 73,000.144 The unemployment rate rose to 6.7%, up 0.2 percentage points from January.144 Services-producing industries lost 56,000 positions. Goods-producing industries lost 28,000, with wholesale and retail trade recording the largest decline at 18,000 jobs.144 The database tracks 1,034 projects currently under construction that depend on labour market conditions.

GDP & Monetary Policy

Real GDP rose 0.1% in January 2026, a second consecutive monthly increase.149 Mining, quarrying, and oil and gas extraction expanded 1.2%. Manufacturing contracted 1.4%.149 The advance estimate indicates 0.2% growth in February.149 Headline CPI fell to 1.8% year-over-year in February — the lowest since early 2021.145 Core measures converged near 2.3-2.4%.145 The Bank of Canada held its overnight rate at 2.25% on March 18, citing weaker near-term growth from US tariffs.67

Trade

The merchandise trade deficit widened to $3.6 billion in January from $1.3 billion in December.143 Motor vehicle and parts exports dropped 21.2% to $5.4 billion — the lowest since September 2021.143 Energy exports partially offset the decline, rising 4.1%.143

Looking Ahead

The April 2 trade data release covers the first full month of the Strait of Hormuz closure. Statistics Canada releases the March Labour Force Survey on April 3.150 The Bank of Canada delivers its next rate decision on April 15, alongside the Monetary Policy Report and March CPI data.69

national.analysis:
Statistics Canada reported real GDP grew 0.1% in January 2026, a second consecutive monthly increase following a flat December.149 Goods-producing industries expanded 0.2%, led by mining, quarrying, and oil and gas extraction, which grew 1.2% in the month.149 Services-producing industries were essentially unchanged. Manufacturing contracted 1.4%, the steepest monthly decline in the current data cycle, reflecting weakness in both durable and non-durable goods production.149 Retail trade GDP rose 0.8%.149 The advance estimate for February indicates 0.2% growth.78 Q4 2025 GDP contracted 0.2% on an annualized basis, while full-year 2025 GDP growth was approximately 1.7%; the IMF projects 1.6% for 2026.13970

The labour market recorded a contraction of 84,000 positions in February, the largest monthly decline since the pandemic recovery period.144 Full-time employment fell 108,000 while part-time employment rose 24,000. Private-sector employment dropped 73,000. The unemployment rate increased to 6.7%, up 0.2 percentage points from January, and the participation rate declined 0.1 percentage points to 64.9%.144 Services-producing industries shed 56,000 positions, with wholesale and retail trade losing 18,000 and other services declining 14,000. Goods-producing industries lost 28,000 positions.14434 Payroll employment from the Survey of Employment, Payrolls and Hours (SEPH) rose 45,600 (+0.2%) in January, providing a contrasting signal from the establishment survey.140

Headline CPI decelerated to 1.8% year-over-year in February 2026, down from 2.3% in January — the lowest reading since early 2021.145 All three Bank of Canada core measures converged: CPI-median at 2.3%, CPI-trim at 2.3%, and CPI-common at 2.4%.145 Food inflation slowed to 5.3% from 7.3% in January.9033 The Bank of Canada held the overnight rate at 2.25% on March 18 — the seventh consecutive meeting at this level following seven cuts from the June 2024 peak of 5.00%.67 Bond markets priced approximately 86% probability of no change at the April 15 meeting.68

Canada's merchandise trade deficit widened to $3.6 billion in January from $1.3 billion in December.143 Total exports fell 4.7% to $62.5 billion; imports declined 1.1% to $66.1 billion. Motor vehicle and parts exports dropped 21.2% to $5.4 billion, the lowest since September 2021, while energy product exports rose 4.1%.14335 Housing starts ran at 250,900 SAAR in February, up 4.5% from 240,148 in January, while the six-month trend declined 0.4% to 256,005 units.89 The average home price stood at $663,828 in February (+1.7% month-over-month).62 Retail sales rose 1.1% to $70.7 billion in January, with motor vehicle dealers leading at +2.0% and general merchandise retailers posting a fourth consecutive monthly increase at +3.0%.14676 Consumer confidence declined to 47.50 in February from 49.30 in January, while the Bloomberg/Nanos index showed a three-week slide into late March.5748

global.analysis:
The Federal Reserve held the federal funds target range at 3.50-3.75% at its March 18 meeting, following three 25-basis-point cuts in late 2025, citing "heightened uncertainty" from geopolitical risk and volatile energy prices.115 The US-Canada policy rate spread stands at 125-150 basis points, maintaining downward pressure on the Canadian dollar — CAD/USD weakened to 0.7198, a two-month low.58 US tariffs on Canadian steel and aluminum exports remain in effect; the Bank of Canada attributed weaker Canadian near-term growth projections partly to these trade disruptions.67

US equity markets were dominated by Strait of Hormuz-related volatility in March. The S&P 500 stood at approximately 6,496 on March 31, down roughly 9.4% from its January 2026 peak.61 Reports of potential US-Iran diplomatic talks on March 31 triggered a broad rally: the S&P 500 gained 2.40%, the Nasdaq 3.24%, and the Dow approximately 2.0% on the session.103 Canada's merchandise trade with the US recorded a 21.2% decline in motor vehicle and parts exports to $5.4 billion in January — the lowest since September 2021 — directly linked to tariff-related disruptions.143

global.analysis:
China's official manufacturing PMI rose to 50.4 in March 2026, crossing above the 50.0 expansion threshold after two months of contraction (49.3 in January, 49.0 in February).105 The non-manufacturing PMI increased to 50.1 from 49.5, with new export orders showing strength.105 The People's Bank of China held the 5-year Loan Prime Rate at 2.90%. China recorded GDP growth of 5.0% for 2025, meeting the official annual target for a second consecutive year. CPI registered +0.2% year-over-year in February, reflecting subdued domestic demand.

China is Canada's second-largest merchandise trading partner, receiving approximately 5% of Canadian merchandise exports annually — crude oil, canola, potash, wood products, and seafood are the primary categories. The return to manufacturing expansion after two months of contraction could affect demand for these Canadian commodity exports through Q2 2026. Higher shipping costs from the Strait of Hormuz closure are affecting input prices for Chinese manufacturers and raising transport costs for Canadian LNG and commodity shipments routed to Asia.37 China controls an estimated 60% of global rare earth mine production and approximately 85% of downstream processing, a factor for Canadian critical minerals projects tracked in the database — the database contains 364 mining projects across Canada.

global.analysis:
The European Central Bank held its deposit facility rate at 2.00% at the March 19 meeting, maintaining its stance as euro area HICP inflation stood at 1.9% year-over-year in Q4 2025 — below the ECB's 2% target.11032 Euro area GDP grew 0.2% quarter-over-quarter in Q4 2025. Germany recorded a second consecutive annual GDP contraction, while Spain and Italy posted comparatively stronger output. Euro area unemployment stood at 5.9%.32

The ECB rate at 2.00% sits 25 basis points below the BoC's 2.25%, creating a narrow differential between the two central banks. The euro strengthened to 1.1460 EUR/USD on March 31 amid geopolitical uncertainty, which indirectly affects Canadian dollar competitiveness in European markets.114 Germany's continued contraction reduces demand for Canadian resource exports to Europe under the CETA (Canada-EU Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement) framework. The Strait of Hormuz closure has introduced energy supply and shipping cost pressures across the eurozone, which may alter trade flow patterns affecting Canadian commodity exporters.

The Bank of England held Bank Rate at 3.75% at its March 18 meeting by unanimous vote, maintaining its stance as UK CPI stood at 2.8% year-over-year in February 2026 — above the BoE's 2% target.72 UK GDP grew 0.1% quarter-over-quarter in Q4 2025, continuing a pattern of subdued output growth. Unemployment stood at 5.2%.128

The BoE rate at 3.75% exceeds the BoC's 2.25% by 150 basis points, reflecting persistent UK inflation relative to Canada's declining CPI trajectory. UK-Canada trade operates under the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership (CPTPP) framework. GBP movements affect pricing for Canadian resource and agri-food exports to the UK. The Strait of Hormuz crisis has elevated energy import costs for the UK, which is a net energy importer, potentially affecting bilateral trade dynamics. The database tracks 7,372 total capital projects across Canada, with UK-linked investment flows most relevant to mining, energy, and financial services sectors.

provinces.name: Ontario
provinces.analysis:
Ontario's unemployment rate rose 0.3 percentage points to 7.6% in February 2026144, the highest level in the province since early 2021, as the labour market absorbed the combined effects of U.S. tariff uncertainty on trade-exposed manufacturing and a slowdown in residential construction activity. Toronto CMA housing starts declined 28% year-over-year in February100, reflecting elevated borrowing costs and reduced buyer qualification volumes. The project database tracks 652 Ontario projects, of which 220 are in rate-sensitive sectors11 — residential, commercial, and mixed-use developments whose timelines are directly linked to financing conditions and mortgage rate movements.

The Ontario 2026 Budget, released March 26, introduced a $210 billion 10-year capital plan — the largest in provincial history — with $37 billion allocated for fiscal year 2026-27.28 Of that total, $63 billion is directed to transit expansion (Ontario Line, Yonge North Subway Extension, Scarborough Subway Extension, Hamilton LRT), $64 billion to health infrastructure covering 50+ hospital projects and approximately 3,000 new beds, and $31 billion to highways including Highway 413 (now under construction) and the Bradford Bypass.10647 The budget projects a $13.8 billion deficit for 2026-27, with total spending of $244.2 billion against revenues of $231.9 billion.28

A temporary HST rebate on new homes is estimated to generate 8,000 housing starts and provide $2.2 billion in joint tax relief.28 The Eglinton Crosstown LRT opened in February 2026, delivering 19 km of rapid transit including 10 km underground.125 The small business corporate income tax rate was reduced from 3.2% to 2.2%, with estimated relief of $1.1 billion to over 375,000 small businesses over three years.28 A $4 billion Protect Ontario Account Investment Fund targets AI, defence, advanced manufacturing, and life sciences.130 The database tracks 150 projects in employment-sensitive sectors (healthcare, education, manufacturing, government) and 205 infrastructure projects in Ontario.11

provinces.name: Quebec
provinces.analysis:
Quebec recorded the largest provincial employment decline in February 2026, shedding 57,000 positions (-1.2%), which pushed the unemployment rate up 0.7 percentage points to 5.9%.144 This represents the steepest single-month job loss in Quebec since the pandemic period. The project database tracks 212 projects in employment-sensitive sectors across the province, including manufacturing, healthcare, and government services.20

The Quebec Budget 2026-27, tabled with a projected $8.6 billion deficit within a $170.8 billion budget, adds $5 billion over six years to infrastructure spending, bringing the 10-year Quebec Infrastructure Plan (QIP) to $167 billion.133 Of the QIP total, $105.8 billion (71%) is designated for asset maintenance, with $3.6 billion for hospitals, $1.2 billion for public transit, and $631 million for higher education.127 An additional $1.7 billion over five years targets economic transformation, including $480 million for critical and strategic minerals.133 The deficit is projected to decline to $1.5 billion by 2028-29.133

Montreal CMA housing starts rose 18% year-over-year in February 2026100, contrasting with the labour market contraction. The database contains 132 rate-sensitive Quebec projects in the residential and commercial pipeline.20 Building permits issued in January 2026 totalled $25.87 billion for residential and $10.27 billion for non-residential categories.144 The REM A3 branch to the West Island is scheduled to open in Q2 2026, and the Quebec City Tramway is under active construction on a 5 km span with operations targeted for 2033.134 The database tracks 493 Quebec projects in total.20

provinces.name: Alberta
provinces.analysis:
Alberta's unemployment rate edged down 0.1 percentage points to 6.3% in February 2026144, as the province's energy sector continued to operate against WTI crude oil at US$102.18/bbl.39 The Alberta Budget 2026, tabled by Finance Minister Nate Horner, projects a $9.4 billion deficit for 2026-27 — more than double the 2025-26 shortfall — driven by a projected $8.8 billion decline in non-renewable resource revenue from 2024-25 levels.64 The budget forecasts WTI at US$60/bbl, compared to a private-sector average of US$58/bbl, and projects oil sands royalties of $9.7 billion and conventional oil royalties of $2.1 billion.64

The three-year capital plan totals $28.3 billion, an increase of $2.2 billion over the previous budget, with $7.1 billion for municipal infrastructure and $4.9 billion for health capital.64 The Trans Mountain pipeline is operating at or near full capacity, with a 10% throughput increase achieved through drag-reducing agents (DRA).138 The Dow Fort Saskatchewan petrochemical complex — a $11.6 billion facility — remains under construction with completion expected by 2029.109 Alberta has also authorized $900 million in borrowing authority for a potential new pipeline to the northern BC coast.64

The project database tracks 727 Alberta projects in total, with 209 energy-sector projects and 243 employment-sensitive projects.21 Alberta's CPI index rose to 202.1 from 201.7 the prior month.144 Two proposed Beacon AI data centre hubs — one in Rocky View County ($100 billion) and one in Leduc County ($100 billion) — are listed in the Alberta Major Projects inventory, representing the scale of AI infrastructure proposals currently in the provincial pipeline.46

provinces.name: British Columbia
provinces.analysis:
British Columbia's unemployment rate held steady at 6.1% in February 2026144, despite employment declining by 20,000 positions over the month, as labour force exits offset the reduction in employment. Vancouver CMA housing starts surged 60% year-over-year in February100, the largest year-over-year increase among major Canadian CMAs, providing a counterpoint to the provincial government's decision to reallocate $1.4 billion from housing programs over three years and close the Community Housing Fund indefinitely.73 The database contains 138 rate-sensitive projects in BC's residential and commercial pipeline.22

BC Budget 2026 projects a $13.3 billion deficit — the largest in provincial history — with nearly $38 billion in capital projects across the fiscal plan.73 Capital commitments include 17 major hospital projects, the Broadway Subway, and the Surrey Langley SkyTrain extension.73 GDP growth is forecast at 1.3% in 2026 and 1.8% in 2027 (TD Economics).36 The province also records the highest-ever forecast for nonresidential construction spending in 2026.73

Manitoba recorded the largest provincial unemployment decline in February 2026, falling 0.6 percentage points to 5.7% from 6.3% the prior month144, despite employment declining by 4,000 positions, as labour force exits exceeded the employment decline. Manitoba Budget 2026, tabled March 25, reports a $498 million deficit — down from $1.7 billion in 2025-26 — with a surplus of $8 million projected for 2027-28.53 The budget includes a record $3.8 billion capital investment plan covering roads, hospitals, schools, and community infrastructure, with a five-year capital plan averaging $4.3 billion annually.53 The PST was removed from groceries effective 2026.52 The database tracks 2,058 Manitoba projects and 616 infrastructure projects.24

The CPI index edged down to 189.5 from 189.6, representing a marginal decline in the price level over the month.144 The project database tracks 339 Nova Scotia projects and 119 energy-sector projects.25

Nova Scotia's Capital Plan 2026-27 is the largest in provincial history at $3.5 billion, with $1.5 billion allocated to the "More, Faster: Action for Health Build" plan.54 Of that healthcare allocation, $1.2 billion is directed to the Halifax Infirmary expansion and Cape Breton Regional Hospital redevelopment.54 An additional $873.8 million targets 5,700 new and replacement long-term care spaces by 2032.54 Budget 2026-27 projects a $1.24 billion deficit, with the debt-to-GDP ratio projected to breach the 40% guardrail by 2027-28.55 Health spending rose 6% to $6.7 billion.55

The Wind West offshore wind project proposes 5 GW of capacity, with Hydro-Quebec issuing a formal request for information to assess feasibility of connecting its grid with Nova Scotia's proposed wind farms.94 Federal defence spending in Nova Scotia includes a $2 billion package, with $1.2 billion allocated to upgrade power and service infrastructure at CFB Halifax Dockyard and Stadacona.93 Public sector headcount reductions are projected to generate $914.3 million in cumulative savings by 2029-30.55

provinces.name: Northwest Territories
provinces.analysis:
The Northwest Territories' unemployment rate rose 0.3 percentage points to 5.3% in February 2026144, as the territory contends with a structural transition in its resource economy. All three producing diamond mines — Diavik (closing 2026), Ekati (2029), and Gahcho Kue (2030) — are scheduled to cease operations by 2030, removing a primary employer and revenue source.137 Employment decreased 3.4% between 2023 and 2024, reflecting the contraction underway.137

NWT Budget 2026-27 totals $2.724 billion with no new taxes introduced.117 The Mining Incentive Program was updated with the $500,000 lifetime cap conditionally removed for corporate projects, while the $1.5 million annual budget was maintained.117 PM Carney announced a $35 billion+ Arctic defence and northern infrastructure plan including $32 billion at Forward Operating Locations in Yellowknife and Inuvik, plus the Mackenzie Highway extension.29

The Mackenzie Valley Highway — an 800+ km route from Wrigley to Norman Wells (Phase 1) and to Inuvik (Phase 2) — received construction approval with work starting summer 2026 and a revised cost estimate exceeding $2 billion.92 The Taltson Hydro Expansion ($2 billion proposed, 60 MW) would double the NWT's hydro capacity and deliver clean power to 11 communities serving approximately 70% of residents.122 The Pine Point zinc-lead mine ($653 million) is under review.49 The project database tracks 188 NWT projects and 52 energy-sector projects.3

provinces.name: Nunavut
provinces.analysis:
Nunavut's unemployment rate fell 3.0 percentage points to 10.8% in February 2026144, the largest single-month decline among all provinces and territories. The rate remains the highest in Canada, reflecting the structural employment constraints of a territory with 25 communities accessible only by air or seasonal sealift. The project database tracks 57 Nunavut projects, with 10 employment-sensitive projects.4

The federal government announced a $32 billion Northern Defence and Infrastructure investment covering Nunavut, including new Forward Operating Locations in Iqaluit and Northern Operation Support Nodes in Cambridge Bay and Rankin Inlet.30 Federal military hubs were also announced for Resolute.30 The federal Build Communities Strong Fund ($51 billion national) includes Nunavut allocations.123

Housing remains a central development constraint. The territory's target is 3,000 new units by 2030 with a $2.6 billion investment.121 The Nunavut 750 Homes Initiative — a tri-party agreement between the Government of Canada ($250 million), Government of Nunavut ($230 million), and Nunavut Tunngavik Incorporated — is under construction, with Baker Lake receiving the first 10 modular homes built by Ottawa manufacturer Caivan.56 Baffinland Iron Mines completed Inuit consultation for the Steensby Component of the Mary River project, clearing the final requirement to advance into construction at an estimated $3 billion.65 The Back River Gold Project ($610 million) is under construction in western Nunavut.49 Agnico Eagle operates as one of Nunavut's largest employers with over 2,000 positions, and gross mineral production exceeds $2.3 billion annually.121

goodsIndustries.analysis:
Agriculture, forestry, fishing and hunting sector GDP stood at $47.2B in December 2025 and declined in January 2026, with decreases in both crop production and forestry.153 Crop production (except cannabis) fell 1.3% in November 2025, while forestry and logging declined 2.8% for the third consecutive month.153 Nutrien (NTR) closed at $104.62, up 50.6% year-over-year but down 1.0% week-over-week, reflecting sustained potash demand alongside near-term price softness.40 Canada exported 22.9 million tonnes of potash in 2024, accounting for over 39% of global exports.75

The project database tracks 17 agricultural projects ($5.47B), anchored by the BHP Jansen potash project in Saskatchewan ($10.6B total for Stage 1 and Stage 2), which is in full-scale construction with 5,500 construction-phase jobs and first production rescheduled to mid-CY2027.75 U.S.-Canada tariff disputes remain a factor for agricultural exports, with Canada's retaliatory tariffs on U.S. goods continuing under the ongoing trade dispute.82 If trade disputes persist, agricultural export volumes face continued exposure to policy-driven disruption.

goodsIndustries.analysis:
Mining, quarrying, and oil and gas extraction sector GDP expanded 1.2% in January 2026, fully offsetting December's decline, led by increased oil and gas extraction activity.153 Sector GDP stood at $119.6B in December 2025.153 WTI crude surged to US$102.88/bbl on March 30 — the first settlement above $100 since July 2022 — driven by the Strait of Hormuz closure disrupting approximately 20 million barrels per day of seaborne oil flows.104 The WCS-WTI differential narrowed from US$15/bbl to US$9.95/bbl.113 The project database tracks 418 mining and energy projects ($275.87B), the largest pipeline by value of any goods sector.97 The Alberta Budget 2026 forecasts WTI at US$60/bbl; at the current settlement of US$102.88/bbl, the gap between market prices and the provincial fiscal assumption stands at approximately US$43/bbl.64

LNG Canada ($40B) in Kitimat loaded its first cargo in June 2025, with Phase 1 capacity at 6.5 million tonnes per annum and marine terminal in-water works scheduled for April 15, 2026.124 Cameco (CCO) traded at $147.75, down 14.1% month-over-month but up 149.9% year-over-year, while the URA ETF (uranium proxy) stood at $46.86, down 17.0% month-over-month but up 114.2% year-over-year.38 U.S. Section 232 tariffs on Canadian steel and aluminum stand at 50%, affecting downstream metal processing and pipeline fabrication across the sector.80

Manufacturing sector GDP stood at $198.0B in December 2025 and contracted 1.4% in January 2026.153 The S&P Global Canada Manufacturing PMI rose to 51.0 in February 2026 from 50.4 in January, a 13-month high, with new orders growing for the first time in 13 months.131 However, export orders continued to decline, though at the slowest pace since October 2025, and 24% of PMI respondents expected output growth, the highest share since December 2024.131 Steel input costs (SLX proxy) at $90.13 fell 10.4% month-over-month, while U.S. Section 232 tariffs on Canadian steel and aluminum remain at 50%.80

Stellantis halted Jeep Compass production plans at Brampton, affecting 3,000 direct jobs, while GM ended BrightDrop production at Ingersoll and scaled back Oshawa operations.87 The federal government announced a $3B Strategic Response Fund and $100M Regional Tariff Response Initiative for automotive manufacturing, with Ottawa reducing GM's tariff-free import quota by 24.2% and Stellantis' by 50%.87 The project database tracks 54 manufacturing projects ($67.39B).153 If the Strategic Response Fund and Regional Tariff Response Initiative deploy as planned, automotive manufacturing would partially offset tariff-related disruption. The food, beverage, and tobacco subsector recorded sales of $187.8B for full-year 2025, an increase of 6.1%, representing a stable component within the broader wholesale decline.147 The Bank of Canada policy rate at 2.25% continues to influence inventory financing costs for wholesale distributors carrying large stock positions.67 No capital projects in the pipeline are directly mapped to NAICS 41. Arts, entertainment and recreation recorded sector GDP of $19,536M in December 2025 — the smallest services-producing NAICS sector.153 Ontario expects moderate to slow employment growth in 2025-2027, while Quebec projects negative job growth in this sector through 2024-2026.153 The sector's labour structure is distinctive: 46.6% of Ontario's sector employees work part-time, compared to 17.6% for all industries, and youth aged 15-24 make up 39.5% of the workforce.153

A $150M BMO Field upgrade is underway in Toronto ahead of the FIFA World Cup in June 2026, representing the sector's most prominent near-term capital project.16 Trade tensions are placing downward pressure on consumer confidence and discretionary spending, which directly affects entertainment and recreation activity levels.153 The project database tracks 150 arts, entertainment, and recreation projects valued at $22.26B, including resort developments, cultural facilities, and sports venues.17

servicesIndustries.name: Accommodation & Food Services
servicesIndustries.analysis:
Accommodation and food services recorded sector GDP of $52,548M in December 2025; no January 2026 month-over-month change was available from Statistics Canada.153 One-third of restaurant establishments were operating at a loss in 2023, and insolvency filings rose by 219 — an increase of 43.8% year-over-year — reflecting persistent financial stress across the food services subsector.18

The sector faces structural labour shortages, with workers leaving for other industries due to unstable hours and compensation levels that do not compete with alternative employment options.18 Moderate employment growth is expected over 2024-2026, constrained by consumer spending pressures and the ongoing labour supply challenge.18 Among accommodation operators, 60% of Canadian travelers now prefer accommodations with sustainable certifications, and over 50% of independent hospitality providers are expected to adopt Hardware-as-a-Service models.18 No capital projects in the pipeline are directly mapped to NAICS 72.

servicesIndustries.name: Other Services (except Public Administration)
servicesIndustries.analysis:
Other services (except public administration) recorded sector GDP of $44,650M in December 2025; no January 2026 directional change was reported by Statistics Canada.153 The sector encompasses motor vehicle repair, personal care services, funeral services, laundry, religious organizations, advocacy groups, and professional associations — a structurally diverse industry whose aggregate trends are difficult to characterize given the range of constituent activities.153

Quebec's other services sector faces pressure from changing consumer habits and competition from digital alternatives, particularly in personal and repair services where online booking platforms and virtual consultations are displacing traditional in-person service models.153 Fuel costs affect the operational economics of mobile repair and maintenance services across Canada, while labour costs in personal services track with broader wage growth in the services-producing sector.153 No capital projects in the pipeline are directly mapped to NAICS 81. No policy actions, procurement awards, or regulatory developments specific to this sector were identified in the current cycle.

servicesIndustries.name: Public Administration
servicesIndustries.analysis:
Public administration recorded sector GDP of $168,378M in December 2025, the fifth-largest NAICS sector.153 As of January 2026, 4.597 million Canadians worked in the public sector, representing 21.8% of total employment.153 The federal government committed to reducing the public service from 368,000 to 330,000 positions, with 9,800 reductions already begun in 2024-2025 under the Refocusing Government Spending initiative.84 A Comprehensive Expenditure Review is projected to decrease by an estimated 16,000 additional FTEs over three years.84

Federal personnel costs stand at an estimated $71.1B in 2024-25 — the largest federal operating expense — with the Parliamentary Budget Officer projecting $76.2B by 2029-30 absent spending restraint.84 The 2026-27 Main Estimates have been tabled, and the Department of Finance released its departmental plan for the fiscal year.88 The project database tracks 234 government and defence projects valued at $565.85B, including defence facilities, government infrastructure, and indigenous community projects.19

industry_executive_summary:
Goods-producing industries recorded mixed results in January 2026. Mining, quarrying, and oil and gas extraction expanded 1.2% month-over-month, while manufacturing contracted 1.4%.153 Construction and utilities both contributed to goods-sector gains. Agriculture declined, with crop production falling 1.3% and forestry and logging down 2.8% for a third consecutive month.153 The Strait of Hormuz closure drove WTI crude to US$102.88/bbl, the highest settlement since July 2022, directly affecting the 418 mining and energy projects tracked in the database.104

Services-producing industries were essentially unchanged in January 2026. Retail trade rose 0.8%, while wholesale trade declined 1.2%.153 Finance and insurance expanded, whereas real estate and professional services contracted. Transportation and warehousing declined, with extreme weather cited as a contributing factor.153 The February Labour Force Survey reported services-producing industries lost 56,000 positions, with wholesale and retail trade recording the largest subsector decline at 18,000 jobs.144 The project database tracks 7,372 projects across all sectors, with 1,034 under construction and 2,528 proposed.

financialMarkets.summary:
The Bank of Canada's Governing Council held the overnight rate at 2.25% on March 18, maintaining its stance following seven consecutive cuts from the June 2024 peak of 5.00%.67 The Governing Council stated it would "proceed carefully" given heightened uncertainty from US tariffs. Bond markets priced approximately 86% probability of no change at the April 15 meeting, with 14% probability of a 25-basis-point increase.68 The Government of Canada 2-year yield stood at 2.95% and the 10-year at 3.58%, producing a 2-10 year spread of 0.63 percentage points. Year-over-year, the yield curve shifted upward across all terms: the 2-year rose from 2.62% and the 10-year from 3.22%.

WTI crude surged to US$102.88/bbl, up more than 50% in March — the first settlement above $100 since July 2022 — driven by the Strait of Hormuz closure disrupting approximately 20 million barrels per day of seaborne oil flows.104 Brent crude settled at US$112.78/bbl, recording the largest monthly gain for the contract since inception in 1988.104 Natural gas (Henry Hub) traded at approximately US$3.05/MMBtu in late March; the EIA projects an average of $3.80 for 2026.11250 Gold declined approximately 14% in March to ~US$4,578/oz, the steepest monthly drop since October 2008, as margin liquidation and USD strength drove sellers.44 Copper traded in a range of US$5.25-$6.01/lb during March.60

The Canadian dollar weakened 1.85% month-over-month to 0.7198 CAD/USD (1.3893 USD/CAD), reflecting the 125-150 basis point spread between the Federal Reserve's 3.50-3.75% target and the BoC's 2.25%.58 The euro traded at 1.1460 EUR/USD, strengthening amid geopolitical uncertainty.114 The S&P/TSX Composite closed at 32,427 on March 31, up 1.54% on the day but down approximately 6% for March, while recording a 28.2% year-over-year gain.59 The S&P 500 closed at approximately 6,496, rallying 2.40% on March 31 — reports of potential US-Iran diplomatic talks contributed to the late-session advance — though the index remained approximately 9.4% below its January 2026 peak.61103

consumer_pulse:
The Conference Board of Canada's consumer confidence index declined to 47.50 in February from 49.30 in January.57 The Bloomberg/Nanos Canadian Confidence Index recorded a three-week slide into late March, with the index moving toward the neutral threshold.48 The proportion of Canadians expecting the economy to strengthen in six months rose from 17% to 26% over the four-week period, according to Nanos Research.48 Rising energy costs — with WTI above $100/bbl for the first time since 2022 — and US trade friction were the most frequently cited sources of consumer anxiety in sentiment tracking.

Retail sales rose 1.1% to $70.7 billion in January, according to Statistics Canada.146 Motor vehicle and parts dealers led the increase at +2.0%, while general merchandise retailers posted a fourth consecutive monthly gain at +3.0%.14676 Core retail sales (excluding gasoline stations and motor vehicle dealers) increased 0.9%. E-commerce sales rose 1.5% to $4.4 billion, representing 6.2% of total retail trade.146 Alberta recorded the largest provincial retail increase at +3.5%, led by motor vehicle sales.76 The advance estimate for February retail sales is +0.9%.146 Statistics Canada's CPI report showed food inflation decelerating to 5.3% from 7.3% in January, while headline inflation fell to 1.8% year-over-year — the lowest since early 2021.14590
